Time-Series Backtesting and Drift: will the model still work next month?¶

The question: a forecasting model is trained on the past and used on the future, so the only honest test is one that never lets the future leak into the past. And even an honestly tested model decays: the world drifts, and the model quietly keeps predicting last year's world. How badly does the usual shuffled cross-validation fool us on time-series data? Does a machine-learning model beat a trivial "same as last week" forecast once we test it honestly? Has the data drifted, which inputs, and what do the standard alarms (the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and the population stability index, PSI) say? How fast does a model frozen in year 1 decay in year 2, and does refitting fix it? And can the drift alarms themselves be trusted? We use two years of daily bicycle rentals from a bike-share system in Washington DC (731 days), where demand grew by 64% in the second year.

How this notebook works. Each section starts with a plain-English explanation, then the code, then a "how to read this" note.

Run it: uv run jupyter lab ML/time-series-backtesting-drift/time_series_backtesting_drift.ipynb, or Run All in any Jupyter. The data (a small UCI zip) download themselves on the first run and it takes about 3 minutes on a CPU.

1. 💡 The simple analogy¶

Imagine a weather forecaster who is graded on yesterday's answers.

  • Shuffled cross-validation is a test with the answer key in the room. If we tear the calendar into random days and ask the forecaster to predict day 100 while he has already seen days 99 and 101, he looks brilliant, because tomorrow is a lot like yesterday. In real life he never sees tomorrow.
  • Walk-forward backtesting is the honest test. Stand at day 365, predict the next 30 days with only the past, then move to day 395 and repeat, like living through the year.
  • Drift is the world changing under the forecaster's feet. A shop that learned from a year with 3,400 customers a day will keep guessing about 3,400 when the street now brings 5,600. A forecaster who refreshes his notes every month keeps up.
  • Drift alarms are smoke detectors: useful, but a toaster (the seasons) can set them off, and a very sensitive one goes off all the time.

2. Setup¶

What: imports and named constants. Why: one place for numbers like the seed, the day on which the walk-forward starts (day 365), the refit step (30 days) and the PSI rules of thumb (0.1 and 0.25) keeps the notebook reproducible and avoids "magic numbers". Everything random uses the fixed seed.

In [1]:
import urllib.request
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

DATA_DIR = Path("data")
OUT_DIR = Path("outputs")
DATA_URL = "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/275/bike+sharing+dataset.zip"
SEED = 365
TARGET = "cnt"  # bicycles rented in a day
FEATURES = [
    "lag1",
    "lag7",
    "rolling7",
    "temp",
    "hum",
    "windspeed",
    "weathersit",
    "holiday",
    "workingday",
    "weekday",
]
FIRST_TEST_DAY = 365  # the walk-forward starts here: all of year 1 is the first training set
STEP = 30  # the model is refitted every 30 days
CUTOFFS = list(range(300, 690, 30))  # the "today" dates used to compare validation schemes
N_BOOTSTRAP = 1_000
PSI_WATCH, PSI_ALARM = 0.1, 0.25  # the industry rules of thumb for the population stability index
TEAL, ORANGE, NAVY, GREY, PURPLE = "#2a9d8f", "#e76f51", "#264653", "#b8bcc2", "#7b5ea7"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
OUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
DATA_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)


def fmt_p(p: float) -> str:
    """Formats a p-value, showing values below floating-point precision honestly.

    Args:
        p: The p-value.

    Returns:
        A short string such as ``3.2e-08`` or ``< 1e-300``.
    """
    return "< 1e-300" if float(p) < 1e-300 else f"{float(p):.1e}"

3. Hypotheses and why we chose each test¶

# Question H₀ (nothing interesting) Hₐ Test
H1 Does shuffled k-fold cross-validation predict the future error as well as walk-forward validation? Both estimates are unbiased Shuffled is too optimistic At 13 "today" dates, compare each scheme's predicted error with the error that really followed; t-test of the bias; paired Wilcoxon of the absolute biases
H2 Do ridge regression and gradient boosting beat the trivial forecasts (same day last week, yesterday) when tested walk-forward? Same absolute error Lower Diebold-Mariano test (errors of neighbouring days are correlated, so the standard error is corrected); week-block bootstrap intervals
H3 Has the data drifted between year 1 and year 2? Same distribution Different Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, chi-square for categories, PSI
H4 Does a model frozen at the end of year 1 decay, and does refitting every 30 days prevent it? Same error Frozen is worse and gets worse Diebold-Mariano test; Spearman correlation of error with time
H5 Do KS and PSI alarms stay quiet when nothing changes, and do they catch real shifts? Few false alarms They depend on the window size and the rule Simulated shifts of 0 to 1 standard deviation in windows of 30, 90 and 365 days; the seasonal check

Why these tests? Time-series errors are autocorrelated (a bad day is often followed by another), so ordinary t-tests would overstate the evidence; the Diebold-Mariano test is the standard fix for comparing two forecasts and uses a robust (Newey-West) standard error. For drift, the KS test compares whole distributions without assumptions, while PSI is the industry's score for "how far has this feature moved?" (below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 worth watching, above 0.25 large).

4. Audit: two years of bicycles¶

What: the Bike Sharing Dataset (Fanaee-T and Gama, UCI): one row per day for 2011 and 2012 with the number of rentals (cnt), the weather (temperature, humidity, wind, a weather type) and calendar flags. We check completeness, how the level changes between the two years, the weekly rhythm and the seasons. Why: every forecasting project should begin by looking at the series: trend, seasonality and gaps decide which validation and which features make sense.

Not in this project's legacy: there is no old code to replace (a new project).

  • A big level shift: the average day had 3,406 rentals in 2011 and 5,600 in 2012, +64%; the 2012 maximum is 8,714 against 6,043 in 2011. This is the "drift" the rest of the notebook is about.

5. Lag features, built without peeking¶

What: to forecast a day we give the model what we would really know the evening before: the rentals yesterday (lag1), a week ago (lag7) and the average of the previous seven days (rolling7, shifted by one day so that it never contains the day itself), plus the weather and calendar of the day (the weather is the observed one, standing in for a good forecast). We drop the first week (no history) and assert that the lags line up. Why: leakage hides in lag features: a rolling mean that includes today is a copy of the answer.

In [3]:
def make_frame(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds features that use only what is known the evening before.

    ``lag1`` and ``lag7`` are the rentals one and seven days earlier and ``rolling7`` is the
    average of the previous seven days (shifted by one day so that today never leaks into
    itself). The weather columns are the observed weather of the day, a stand-in for a
    weather forecast.

    Args:
        frame: One row per day in date order.

    Returns:
        The frame with the lag features; the first week (which has no history) is dropped and a
        day counter ``t`` is added.
    """
    out = frame.copy()
    out["lag1"] = out[TARGET].shift(1)
    out["lag7"] = out[TARGET].shift(7)
    out["rolling7"] = out[TARGET].shift(1).rolling(7).mean()
    out = out.dropna(subset=["lag1", "lag7", "rolling7"]).reset_index(drop=True)
    out["t"] = np.arange(len(out))
    return out


days = make_frame(raw)
assert days.loc[10, "lag1"] == raw[TARGET].iloc[16] and days.loc[10, "lag7"] == raw[TARGET].iloc[10]
print(f"{len(days)} usable days; the model sees {len(FEATURES)} features: {', '.join(FEATURES)}")
print(
    "Correlation of today's rentals with: "
    + ", ".join(
        f"{c} {days[TARGET].corr(days[c]):+.2f}"
        for c in ("lag1", "lag7", "rolling7", "temp", "hum", "windspeed")
    )
)

724 usable days; the model sees 10 features: lag1, lag7, rolling7, temp, hum, windspeed, weathersit, holiday, workingday, weekday
Correlation of today's rentals with: lag1 +0.85, lag7 +0.76, rolling7 +0.85, temp +0.62, hum -0.11, windspeed -0.24

How to read this:

  • 724 usable days and 10 features; the assertion confirms that each lag really comes from before the day.
  • The recent past is the best predictor: today's rentals correlate +0.85 with yesterday's and with the previous week's average, +0.76 with the same weekday a week earlier, and +0.62 with temperature; humidity (-0.11) and wind (-0.24) matter less.

6. The models and the walk-forward machinery¶

What: four forecasters. Two baselines that learn nothing: same day last week (lag 7) and yesterday (lag 1). Two learners: a ridge regression (a straight-line model with a penalty on large weights, features standardised) and gradient boosting (an ensemble of decision trees). Every forecast comes from forecast(name, train, test): it may only look at train. walk_forward repeats it: fit on days up to t, predict the next 30 days, move on. diebold_mariano compares two forecasts with a robust standard error. Why: a function that is physically unable to see the test rows is the simplest guarantee of a leak-free evaluation.

In [4]:
def make_model(name: str):
    """A forecasting model by name (``None`` for the two baselines that need no fitting)."""
    if name == "ridge":
        return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), RidgeCV(alphas=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000]))
    if name == "gradient boosting":
        return HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=200, random_state=SEED)
    return None


BASELINES = {"same day last week (lag 7)": "lag7", "yesterday (lag 1)": "lag1"}


def forecast(name: str, train: pd.DataFrame, test: pd.DataFrame) -> np.ndarray:
    """Predictions for ``test`` from a model fitted on ``train`` only.

    Args:
        name: ``ridge``, ``gradient boosting`` or one of the baseline names.
        train: The days the model may learn from.
        test: The days to predict.

    Returns:
        One prediction per test day.
    """
    if name in BASELINES:
        return test[BASELINES[name]].to_numpy()
    model = make_model(name).fit(train[FEATURES], train[TARGET])
    return model.predict(test[FEATURES])


def walk_forward(
    name: str,
    frame: pd.DataFrame,
    first: int = FIRST_TEST_DAY,
    step: int = STEP,
    retrain: bool = True,
    last: int | None = None,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Walk-forward validation: fit on the past, predict the next ``step`` days, then move on.

    Args:
        name: Model name.
        frame: The days.
        first: Index of the first day to predict.
        step: Days predicted before the model is (optionally) refitted.
        retrain: If False the model is fitted once, on the days before ``first``.
        last: Stop before this day index (default: the end of the data).

    Returns:
        A table with the day ``t``, the actual rentals, the prediction and the absolute error.
    """
    end = len(frame) if last is None else last
    rows = []
    for start in range(first, end, step):
        train_end = start if retrain else first
        part = frame.iloc[start : min(start + step, end)]
        pred = forecast(name, frame.iloc[:train_end], part)
        rows.append(
            pd.DataFrame(
                {
                    "t": part["t"].to_numpy(),
                    "actual": part[TARGET].to_numpy(),
                    "predicted": pred,
                    "error": part[TARGET].to_numpy() - pred,
                }
            )
        )
    out = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
    out["abs_error"] = out["error"].abs()
    return out


def diebold_mariano(loss_a: np.ndarray, loss_b: np.ndarray, lags: int = 7) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Do two forecasts have the same average loss? (Diebold-Mariano test with robust errors.)

    Neighbouring days have related errors, so the standard error uses a Newey-West correction.

    Args:
        loss_a: Daily loss (absolute error) of forecast A.
        loss_b: Daily loss of forecast B.
        lags: Number of days of error correlation allowed for.

    Returns:
        The mean loss difference (A minus B) and its two-sided p-value.
    """
    diff = loss_a - loss_b
    fit = sm.OLS(diff, np.ones(len(diff))).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": lags})
    return float(diff.mean()), float(fit.pvalues[0])


print("Models: two baselines (no learning), a ridge regression and gradient boosting.")

Models: two baselines (no learning), a ridge regression and gradient boosting.

How to read this: the models and tools are defined. A baseline needs no fitting, which makes it the fair yardstick: if a clever model cannot beat "yesterday", it has learned nothing useful.

7. H1: does shuffled cross-validation lie?¶

What: we stand at 13 different "today" dates (day 300, 330, ..., 660). At each, we ask two validation schemes, using only the days before today, how large the error over the next 30 days will be: shuffled 5-fold cross-validation (random days held out, the habit of tabular machine learning) and walk-forward validation (expanding window, predict the following 30 days, repeat). Then we really fit on all days before today, predict the next 30 days and record the error that happened. The difference between the promise and what happened is the bias of the scheme. Why: any scheme can be judged by whether its promises come true.

In [5]:
def kfold_mae(name: str, frame: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    """The mistake rate a *shuffled* 5-fold cross-validation reports."""
    errors = []
    for fit_idx, val_idx in KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED).split(frame):
        pred = forecast(name, frame.iloc[fit_idx], frame.iloc[val_idx])
        errors.append(np.abs(frame[TARGET].iloc[val_idx].to_numpy() - pred).mean())
    return float(np.mean(errors))


def walk_forward_mae(name: str, frame: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    """The mistake rate a walk-forward (expanding-window) validation reports on the same days."""
    return float(walk_forward(name, frame, first=120, step=STEP)["abs_error"].mean())


rows = []
for cutoff in CUTOFFS:
    past, future = days.iloc[:cutoff], days.iloc[cutoff : cutoff + STEP]
    for name in ("ridge", "gradient boosting"):
        realised = np.abs(future[TARGET].to_numpy() - forecast(name, past, future)).mean()
        rows.append(
            {
                "cutoff day": cutoff,
                "model": name,
                "realised": realised,
                "shuffled k-fold says": kfold_mae(name, past),
                "walk-forward says": walk_forward_mae(name, past),
            }
        )
leak = pd.DataFrame(rows)
leak["shuffled bias"] = leak["shuffled k-fold says"] - leak["realised"]
leak["walk-forward bias"] = leak["walk-forward says"] - leak["realised"]
print(
    f"At each of {len(CUTOFFS)} 'today' dates we ask both validation schemes how large the "
    f"next {STEP} days' error will be, then check:"
)
summary = (
    leak.groupby("model")[
        [
            "realised",
            "shuffled k-fold says",
            "walk-forward says",
            "shuffled bias",
            "walk-forward bias",
        ]
    ]
    .mean()
    .round(0)
)
print(summary.to_string())
for name, group in leak.groupby("model"):
    a, b = group["shuffled bias"].to_numpy(), group["walk-forward bias"].to_numpy()
    ta = stats.ttest_1samp(a, 0.0)
    ci = stats.t.interval(0.95, len(a) - 1, loc=a.mean(), scale=stats.sem(a))
    wil = stats.wilcoxon(np.abs(a), np.abs(b))
    print(
        f"{name}: shuffled k-fold is off by {a.mean():+.0f} rentals on average "
        f"(95% CI {ci[0]:+.0f} to {ci[1]:+.0f}; t-test against zero p = {fmt_p(ta.pvalue)}), "
        f"walk-forward by {b.mean():+.0f}; the shuffled error is larger in "
        f"{int((np.abs(a) > np.abs(b)).sum())} of {len(a)} cut-offs (Wilcoxon p = "
        f"{fmt_p(wil.pvalue)})"
    )

for name, color, marker in [("ridge", TEAL, "o"), ("gradient boosting", ORANGE, "s")]:

    ax.plot(

        sub["shuffled bias"],

        marker=marker,
        lw=2,

        sub["walk-forward bias"],
        color=color,
        marker=marker,
        lw=2,
        ls="--",
        alpha=0.6,
        label=f"{name}: walk-forward",
    )
ax.axhline(0, color=NAVY, lw=1.2)
ax.set_xlabel("'Today' (day number); the validation sees only earlier days")
ax.set_ylabel("Predicted error minus the error that really happened (rentals)")
ax.set_title(
    "Shuffled cross-validation promises an error far smaller than the future delivers",
    loc="left",
    fontweight="bold",
    fontsize=11,

How to read this:

  • Shuffled cross-validation promises too little error: for gradient boosting it predicts a mean error of 439 rentals while 707 really followed: a bias of -267 rentals (95% CI -415 to -119; t-test against zero p = 0.002). For ridge: promise 519, reality 686, bias -167 (CI -280 to -54; p = 0.007).
  • Walk-forward is closer, but not perfect: its bias is -153 (boosting) and -88 (ridge). It is still optimistic because demand was growing: the past is easier than the future when the world drifts (H3 and H4).
  • The shuffled error is larger than the walk-forward error in 11 of 13 cut-offs for boosting (Wilcoxon p = 0.02) and in 10 of 13 for ridge (p = 0.22, not significant with 13 cut-offs). We reject H₀ for boosting; for ridge the direction is the same but the evidence is weaker.
  • Why does shuffling cheat? Held-out day 100 has neighbours (days 99 and 101) in the training set, and with lag features those neighbours contain its answer. The model is graded on problems it has effectively seen.

8. H2: do the models beat a trivial forecast, honestly tested?¶

What: the walk-forward evaluation of year 2 (359 days, refitting every 30 days with an expanding window) for the four forecasters, with the mean absolute error (MAE), the percentage error (MAPE) and a bootstrap interval that resamples whole weeks (to respect the correlation between days). Each learner is compared with the baselines using the Diebold-Mariano test. Why: the honest question is not "is the model accurate?" but "is it better than doing nothing clever?".

In [7]:
MODELS = ["same day last week (lag 7)", "yesterday (lag 1)", "ridge", "gradient boosting"]
walk = {name: walk_forward(name, days) for name in MODELS}
weeks = (walk["ridge"]["t"] - FIRST_TEST_DAY) // 7
rows = []
for name, frame in walk.items():
    block_means = frame.groupby(weeks.to_numpy())["abs_error"].mean().to_numpy()
    boots = [rng.choice(block_means, len(block_means)).mean() for _ in range(N_BOOTSTRAP)]
    rows.append(
        {
            "model": name,
            "MAE": frame["abs_error"].mean(),
            "low": np.percentile(boots, 2.5),
            "high": np.percentile(boots, 97.5),
            "MAPE": (frame["abs_error"] / frame["actual"]).mean() * 100,
        }
    )
board = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model")
n_test = len(walk["ridge"])
print(
    f"Walk-forward over {n_test} days (refit every {STEP} days, expanding window); "
    "intervals resample whole weeks:"
)
print(board.round(1).to_string())
for a in ("ridge", "gradient boosting"):
    for b in ("yesterday (lag 1)", "same day last week (lag 7)"):
        diff, p = diebold_mariano(walk[a]["abs_error"].to_numpy(), walk[b]["abs_error"].to_numpy())
        print(
            f"{a} minus {b}: {diff:+.0f} rentals of absolute error per day "
            f"(Diebold-Mariano p = {fmt_p(p)})"
        )
diff, p = diebold_mariano(
    walk["gradient boosting"]["abs_error"].to_numpy(), walk["ridge"]["abs_error"].to_numpy()
)
print(f"gradient boosting minus ridge: {diff:+.0f} (p = {fmt_p(p)})")

  • Both learners beat "same day last week" clearly: ridge by 378 rentals a day (Diebold-Mariano p = 1e-10), boosting by 350 (p = 7e-8).
  • Against "yesterday" the win is smaller: ridge is 145 better (p = 3e-4); boosting is 116 better but only borderline (p = 0.051). We reject H₀ for ridge, and only narrowly for boosting.
  • The two learners are tied: boosting minus ridge is +29 rentals (p = 0.47). A straight line on the recent past is as good as a forest of trees here.
  • A warning about the percentages: MAPE looks poor (63% to 119%) because some days have very few rentals (one day in 2012 had 22), and a percentage of a tiny number is huge. The MAE is more informative.

9. H3: has the data drifted?¶

What: year 1 (days 0 to 364) is the reference; year 2 is the current data. For each numeric variable we run a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (the largest gap between the two cumulative distributions) and compute the PSI with 10 bins from the reference. For the categorical variables (weather type, working day, holiday) we use a chi-square test and Cramér's V. We also track the rolling PSI of the last 90 days against year 1. The target (cnt) and the lags, which carry the target, are included. Why: drift monitoring asks which inputs have moved, because that tells you what to look at.

In [9]:
def psi(reference: np.ndarray, current: np.ndarray, bins: int = 10) -> float:
    """Population stability index: how far has a distribution moved from the reference?

    The reference is cut into ``bins`` equally populated bins; PSI sums (share_now - share_then)
    times the log of their ratio over the bins. Under 0.1 is usually read as stable, 0.1 to 0.25
    as a shift worth watching and above 0.25 as a large shift.

    Args:
        reference: Values from the reference period.
        current: Values from the period being checked.
        bins: Number of reference-quantile bins.

    Returns:
        The PSI (0 means identical shares in every bin).
    """
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(reference, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    ref = np.histogram(reference, edges)[0] / len(reference)
    cur = np.histogram(current, edges)[0] / len(current)
    ref, cur = np.clip(ref, 1e-4, None), np.clip(cur, 1e-4, None)
    return float(((cur - ref) * np.log(cur / ref)).sum())


reference, current = days[days["t"] < FIRST_TEST_DAY], days[days["t"] >= FIRST_TEST_DAY]
rows = []
for col in ["cnt", "lag1", "lag7", "rolling7", "temp", "hum", "windspeed"]:
    ks = stats.ks_2samp(reference[col], current[col])
    rows.append(
        {
            "variable": col,
            "reference mean": reference[col].mean(),
            "current mean": current[col].mean(),
            "KS statistic": ks.statistic,
            "KS p-value": fmt_p(ks.pvalue),
            "PSI": psi(reference[col].to_numpy(), current[col].to_numpy()),
        }
    )
for col in ["weathersit", "workingday", "holiday"]:
    table = pd.crosstab(
        pd.concat([reference, current])[col], np.r_[np.zeros(len(reference)), np.ones(len(current))]
    )
    chi2, p, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
    rows.append(
        {
            "variable": col + " (categories)",
            "reference mean": reference[col].mean(),
            "current mean": current[col].mean(),
            "KS statistic": np.sqrt(chi2 / table.values.sum()),
            "KS p-value": fmt_p(p),
            "PSI": np.nan,
        }
    )
drift = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("variable")
print(
    f"Reference: days 0-{FIRST_TEST_DAY - 1} ({len(reference)} days); current: the next "
    f"{len(current)} days. (For categories the 'KS statistic' column holds Cramer's V.)"
)
print(drift.round(3).to_string())

How to read this:

  • The target and its lags drifted enormously: the mean of cnt moved from 3,437 to 5,651; KS statistic 0.61 (p = 1e-63) and PSI 1.93 (the alarm line is 0.25); the lags and the weekly rolling mean show the same (PSI 1.93 to 3.17). We reject H₀ for the demand level.
  • The weather barely moved: temperature (KS p = 0.21), wind (p = 0.11) and weather type (p = 0.15) show no significant change; humidity gives p = 0.03 (not significant after correcting for the seven tests; the Bonferroni threshold is 0.007). The calendar variables are identical.
  • But PSI calls the weather "worth watching": temperature has a PSI of 0.104 and humidity 0.117, just above the 0.1 line, although the KS test sees nothing (temperature): PSI is a rule of thumb, not a test, and it is noisy (see H5).
  • The right question is what moves the target, not the inputs: the drift here is in demand (growth of the service), not in the weather, and a monitor watching only the inputs would have missed it. The rolling PSI figure shows the demand drifting away from year 1 and the weather wobbling with the seasons.

10. H4: does a frozen model decay, and does refitting help?¶

What: two ways of running each learner through year 2. Frozen: fitted once on year 1 and never again (the model that is deployed and forgotten); it still receives the fresh lag features every day. Refitted: refitted every 30 days on all the data so far (what we did in H2). We compare the mean absolute errors by month, test the difference with Diebold-Mariano and ask whether the frozen model's error grows with time (Spearman correlation). Why: it measures the price of not monitoring.

In [11]:

How to read this:

  • The frozen boosting model is badly hurt: its mean error in year 2 is 1,632 rentals against 762 when refitted, a difference of 870 a day (Diebold-Mariano p = 1e-18); its error grows with time (Spearman +0.40, p = 2e-15) and reaches 2,465 in September. We reject H₀.
  • The reason is simple: the best day of year 1 had 6,043 rentals, and 49% of the days of year 2 were busier. A tree can only predict values it has seen in training, so the frozen model under-predicts on 91% of the days and cannot follow the growth.
  • Ridge, a straight line in the lags, copes much better: frozen error 899 against 733 refitted (a still significant difference of 166 a day, p = 5e-9); its error also grows with time but more gently (Spearman +0.22).
  • Refitting every month fixes most of it for both models: from April on the refitted errors stay between about 450 and 1,000, while the frozen boosting model's rise to 1,500 to 2,500 (March, 1,275 for boosting, is the one hard month for everybody).
  • The lesson: in the presence of drift, a model that extrapolates (linear) degrades more gracefully than one that cannot (trees), and refitting on a schedule is the cheapest drift defence.

11. H5: can the drift alarms be trusted?¶

What: two tests of the alarms themselves. (a) For temperature, we draw a window of 30, 90 or 365 days from the reference, shift it by 0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0 standard deviations, and count how often the KS test (p < 0.05) and the PSI rules (above 0.1; above 0.25) raise an alarm: with shift 0 this is the false alarm rate, with a shift it is the power. (b) Seasonality: no sensor changed during year 1, yet we compare each month of year 1 with the other months. Why: an alarm that cries wolf is switched off, and one that stays silent during real drift is useless.

In [13]:
def detection_rates(
    values: np.ndarray, sizes: list[int], shifts: list[float], reps: int = 400
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """How often do the KS test and the PSI rule raise an alarm when a variable shifts?

    A window of ``size`` values is drawn from the reference, then moved by ``shift`` reference
    standard deviations. The KS test alarms at p < 0.05; the PSI rule alarms at PSI > 0.25
    ("large shift") or PSI > 0.1 ("worth watching").

    Args:
        values: The reference sample.
        sizes: Window sizes (days) to try.
        shifts: Shifts to try, in standard deviations of the reference (0 = no drift).
        reps: Random windows per setting.

    Returns:
        Alarm rates for each window size and shift.
    """
    sd, rows = values.std(), []
    for n in sizes:
        for shift in shifts:
            ks = psi_watch = psi_alarm = 0
            for _ in range(reps):
                window = rng.choice(values, n) + shift * sd
                ks += stats.ks_2samp(values, window).pvalue < 0.05
                p = psi(values, window)
                psi_watch += p > PSI_WATCH
                psi_alarm += p > PSI_ALARM
            rows.append(
                {
                    "window (days)": n,
                    "shift (sd)": shift,
                    "KS alarms": ks / reps,
                    "PSI > 0.1": psi_watch / reps,
                    "PSI > 0.25": psi_alarm / reps,
                }
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

)

How to read this:

  • KS is well behaved: with no shift it alarms in about 3%, 2% and 0% of the windows of 30, 90 and 365 days (at or below the 5% promised; the windows are drawn from the reference itself, which makes the test conservative). It reaches 94% power for a quarter-standard-deviation shift with a year of data, but only 15% with 30 days and 40% with 90 days.
  • PSI is noisy in small windows: with no shift, PSI above 0.1 alarms in 98% of the 30-day windows and 47% of the 90-day windows, and PSI above 0.25 in 66% of the 30-day windows. With a year of data both are quiet (0%). A fixed PSI threshold means different things at different window sizes.
  • A loose PSI rule catches everything and a strict one catches little in small samples: with 365 days PSI above 0.25 detects only 4% of the quarter-sigma shifts but 100% of the half-sigma ones; with 30 days it alarms 88% of the time even for a quarter-sigma shift, but it did so at 66% with no shift at all.
  • Seasonality looks like drift: comparing each month of year 1 with the other months, the KS test alarms in 12 of 12 months and PSI above 0.1 in 12 of 12, although nothing changed. Drift monitors must compare like with like (the same season of the previous year) or remove the seasonal pattern first. We reject H₀ for PSI in small windows and for seasonal data.

12. 🎯 Takeaways¶

  1. Shuffled cross-validation overstates skill on time series: it promised an error of 439 rentals where 707 followed (bias -267, CI -415 to -119); walk-forward promised 554 (bias -153).
  2. Even walk-forward is optimistic when the world drifts, because the past is easier than a growing future.
  3. Beat a trivial baseline before celebrating: ridge reduces the error by 145 rentals a day against "yesterday" (p = 3e-4) and 378 against "same day last week"; gradient boosting is a tie with ridge (p = 0.47).
  4. Drift can sit in the target, not in the inputs: demand rose 64% (PSI 1.93) while temperature, wind and weather type did not move significantly.
  5. A frozen model decays: boosting trained on year 1 has an error of 1,632 against 762 when refitted, and under-predicts on 91% of the days, because trees cannot predict beyond what they have seen; ridge decays far less (899 against 733).
  6. Refit on a schedule: monthly refitting recovered most of the loss.
  7. Alarms need care: KS keeps its false alarm rate (about 3% or less) but needs a year of data to see a quarter-sigma shift; PSI above 0.1 cries wolf in 98% of 30-day windows; and seasonality alone makes every month look "drifted".

13. ⚠️ Limitations¶

  • One series, one city, two years. The drift here is a growth of the service, an unusually clean case; real drift is messier and often gradual.
  • The weather features are observed, not forecast, which flatters every model equally; a real system would use forecasts and have larger errors.
  • Walk-forward with an expanding window is one design; sliding windows, longer gaps between training and test, and different refit schedules would give different numbers.
  • Only 13 cut-offs in H1, so the evidence on the validation schemes is modest (the ridge result is not significant on its own).
  • Gradient boosting was used with default-like settings, and no model was tuned; tuned models and sequence models may behave differently.
  • The drift windows in H5 are drawn from the reference itself, so the KS false alarm rate is lower than the nominal 5%; with real, independent windows it would be closer to 5%.
  • PSI depends on the number of bins (10 here) and the window size; the 0.1 and 0.25 thresholds are conventions from credit scoring, not laws.
  • Seasonality was not removed in the drift checks (that is the point of H5b), and a real monitor should handle it.
  • The daily total hides intraday patterns; the hourly data of the same source would give a harder, richer problem.
